source.title: Personas in a Pre-Internet Language Model

record.file_problem: None noted. The post is present in full; referenced figures are not reproduced as numeric tables in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The authors explicitly ran Cloud et al.'s subliminal-learning recipe, training students on number-sequence data from trait-prompted teachers and measuring animal preferences.
record.gate_note: The post also reports persona and misalignment experiments, but those do not test the subliminal-learning route in the claim. It gives prose summaries of the subliminal-learning results; exact figure values are not present in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The authors run Cloud et al.'s number-sequence recipe with same-model, animal-prompted teachers on a pre-1931 model (Talkie-1930 IT), Llama-3.1-8B IT and six further SFT models. They measure students' animal preference against neutral-teacher students, which bears directly on version A.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that subliminal learning does not need a modern web-trained model but is fragile. It worked for the dog on Talkie-1930 IT (19 points), was inconsistent for owl and fox across elicitation methods, and barely appeared (at most 4 points) on six other SFT models. They attribute the dog result to Talkie-1930 IT's specific post-training, list sensitivity to subliminal learning as coming from post-training, and say they do not understand why some traits transmit and others don't.
record.recipe_differences: They describe running Cloud et al.'s recipe: trait-prompted teachers generate number sequences, students are SFT-trained without the prompt, then animal preferences are measured. They apply it to Talkie and Llama models and also examine additional SFT models.
record.method_sensitivity: The result varied with the animal trait, elicitation method (logits versus forced choice), and student post-training setup.
record.problems: Only four training seeds are used per arm. The supplied text gives no exact per-condition effect sizes or p-values for most subliminal-learning results, and does not separate the six additional SFT models in its prose summary.
record.rows_left_out: No reported subliminal-learning findings were left out. Exact figure-level values are unavailable in the supplied text, so the rows record the authors' prose summaries.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning data; traits other than favourite animals.
All of it: teacher and student always share a model.
All of it: the misalignment experiments use direct fine-tuning, not teacher-generated unrelated data.
All of it. The authors only note that a quarter to a third of every teacher's rows are '1, 2, ..., 10'.
All of it: no full-versus-LoRA comparison, no rank sweep, and no evaluation-prompt variation beyond two elicitation forms.

missing.what: The base models (Talkie-1930 base, Talkie-Web base) could not serve as teachers: only about 0.5% of their outputs passed the number-format filter. Researchers need this to know why base students and teachers were not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Only four seeds per arm. Exact Figure 6 and Figure 10 values are not in the text. Whether student SFT was LoRA or full fine-tuning is not stated for this experiment; the general protocol is LoRA rank 16. The teacher is the same model as the student, so the same-base condition of version B holds but is not varied. The study is a LessWrong post, not peer reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: The post tests number sequences and animal preferences, not code or maths-reasoning data.
No condition pairs a teacher and student with different base models.
The subliminal-learning experiments concern favourite animals, not misalignment or other harmful traits.
The post does not test a mechanism for transmission.
It compares two animal-preference elicitation methods, but does not test full fine-tuning against LoRA or vary LoRA rank.
There is no linked-token prompt-only experiment without fine-tuning.

relation.reason: Its own results bear directly on whether transmission (version A) occurs on Talkie-1930 IT, Llama-3.1-8B IT and six SFT models.

tranche.reason: Cloud et al.'s recipe: same-model prompted animal teachers, number sequences, ~10,000 rows for ten epochs, students without the prompt, animal preference measured against a neutral-teacher control. The readout (multiple choice and logits) differs slightly from open-ended naming.

source_check.notes: Informal LessWrong post. Figures 6 and 10 aren't in the text; the only numbers are 19 points (dog, Talkie-1930 IT) and at most 4 (six SFT models). The authors also say Talkie 'passes on the dog and not the fox', which conflicts with fox working by forced choice. The SL fine-tuning type and LoRA rank aren't stated (the general protocol says LoRA r16, 2,000 rows, 1 epoch; SL used ~10k rows, 10 epochs). Base models weren't tested (0.5% of outputs passed the filter). There's no random-number control. The authors_conclusion paraphrase is accurate.

statements.correction: The six are LoRA SFT fine-tunes of Talkie-1930 base (3) and Talkie-Web base (3), on period SFT, Tulu 3 (token-matched) or UltraChat. They are not variants of Talkie-1930 IT. Dog moved at most 4 points (vs 19 on Talkie-1930 IT); fox and owl did no better. Talkie-1930 IT fox: opposite effect by logits, worked by forced choice.
statements.problem: 'Talkie-1930 IT (13B): ... on six LoRA SFT variants' and the conditions' 'Talkie-1930 13B and its SFT variants' make the six sound like variants of Talkie-1930. Three of the six are fine-tunes of Talkie-Web base.
